title: Private sector and public sector objectives
notes: Authored 2026-10-06 under standard v0.2.0-draft. All claims are provenance generated_gap, verification unverified.

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Compare the objectives of private sector and public sector enterprises, and explain why ownership drives the difference between them.

blocks.heading: Private and public sector objectives
blocks.text: Private sector businesses are owned by individuals or shareholders; public sector enterprises are owned and controlled by the state. Ownership drives the objectives. A private owner keeps the profit, so private businesses are led by profit, survival and growth - though a private business may add social aims, as social enterprises do. The public owner is the state, answerable to the public, so a public enterprise is judged on service: supplying water or transport to every town including remote ones a private firm would find unprofitable, keeping prices affordable, and covering its costs rather than maximising profit. A public enterprise may still earn a surplus from its trading, but the surplus is a means to keep the service running, not the measure of success.

blocks.heading: Two water businesses
blocks.text:
Compare two ways of supplying water to a Namibian town. Kalahari Springs is a private company: it bottles water, sells it where the margin is best, and measures itself on profit and growth. The town's public water utility answers to the state: it must pipe water to every household, including distant settlements where each connection costs far more than it earns, and it is judged on whether the water flows and the price stays affordable.

The utility's objective - a reliable service for all - comes from who owns it; so does the bottler's objective of profit. The same difference appears with the French state railway, which keeps loss-making rural routes running because access, not profit, is its objective.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Topic 1.4 sets out the full range of business ownership, from sole traders to public corporations, of which this comparison is one thread. Topic 6.1 shows how government aims such as employment shape what public enterprises are asked to do, and Topic 6.2 adds the ethical expectations that press on private and public sector alike.
